analysis.one_liner: Bans piece-rate pay in garment factories and makes fashion brands liable for wage theft in their supply chains.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have ended piece-rate pay and made brands legally responsible for garment workers' unpaid wages, was referred to the Senate HELP Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The FABRIC Act would have banned paying garment workers by the piece, guaranteed them at least the federal hourly minimum wage, and made the brands that hire garment factories jointly liable when contractors fail to pay workers. It also would have required garment manufacturers and contractors to register annually with the Labor Department, created a new Labor Department office for the garment industry, and set up a $50 million grant program to support domestic garment manufacturing. The bill never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Garment workers — disproportionately immigrant women in shops sewing for major brands — gain an hourly wage floor instead of piece rates, and a way to collect unpaid wages directly from the brands at the top of their supply chain rather than only from small contractors that may shut down or disappear. Compliant domestic garment manufacturers and workforce nonprofits would also gain access to competitive grants of up to $5 million each, with priority for unionized, minority-owned, women-owned, veteran-owned, and long-established shops.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits employers in the garment industry from paying workers by the piece or unit and requires an hourly wage of at least the federal minimum, while still allowing incentive bonuses on top.

Makes any brand or company contracting for garment manufacturing a 'brand guarantor' that shares joint and several liability for wage violations committed by its contractors and subcontractors, with lost wages plus an equal amount in liquidated damages available to workers.

Requires every garment manufacturer and contractor to register annually with the Labor Department — verifying owners' identities, workers' compensation coverage, and any wage-law violations in the previous three years — with civil penalties of up to $50 million for violations of the registration requirements.

Creates an Office of the Garment Industry at the Labor Department headed by an Undersecretary, and authorizes a $50 million grant program for domestic garment manufacturers and workforce nonprofits, prioritizing unionized shops and minority-, women-, and veteran-owned businesses.
Preserves an exemption for workers covered by bona fide union contracts that meet higher wage standards and include a wage-dispute process.

analysis.who_pays: Fashion brands and retailers would bear new legal exposure: as 'brand guarantors' they could be sued for wage violations anywhere in their contractor chains, giving them a financial stake in policing their suppliers. Garment contractors and manufacturers would bear registration, recordkeeping, and compliance costs, annual fees starting at $200, and the loss of piece-rate pay systems. Some of these costs would likely show up in clothing prices or in pressure to move production overseas, and taxpayers would fund roughly $75 million in authorized spending for the new office and grant program.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fashion brands, garment contractors, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The registration regime is heavy: shops must submit names, home addresses, and Social Security numbers of every owner, officer, major shareholder, and all production employees, and face civil penalties of up to $50 million — a compliance burden that falls hardest on small contractors.

Banning piece rates could reduce earnings for the fastest, most productive sewers who currently out-earn an hourly wage; the bill preserves incentive bonuses but does not guarantee they replace piece-rate earnings.

Joint liability plus strict registration could push brands to shift production to other countries rather than absorb the cost of policing U.S. contractors, which would hurt the very workers the bill aims to protect; the bill's $50 million in domestic manufacturing grants is partly an attempt to counteract that.

The bill authorizes about $75 million in new federal spending ($10 million plus $3 million a year for the new office, and $50 million for grants), and the office's first-year authorization is still dated fiscal year 2022, a leftover from an earlier version.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefits are real and targeted at a documented problem: garment work has a long history of below-minimum piece-rate earnings and wage theft by small contractors that vanish before workers can collect. Making brands jointly liable goes after the money at the top of the chain. The costs fall on brands and contractors in the form of legal exposure and paperwork, and the main good-faith worry is that the industry responds by leaving the country instead of complying — a risk the bill's grant program tries to offset but cannot guarantee. On balance the provisions for workers are stronger and more central than the costs, though the registration requirements could have been scaled to shop size.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the FABRIC Act in the Senate on September 14, 2023, with Senators Booker, Feinstein, Padilla, Sanders, and Warren as original cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions — the standard first step for a Senate labor bill.
Eleven senators — 10 of the 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of the 4 Independents — cosponsored the bill. No Republican signed on.

In the roughly 16 months remaining in the Congress, the HELP Committee held no hearing, took no markup vote, and reported nothing; the bill never reached the Senate floor, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Apparel brands and garment contractors are better off because the bill died: they face no joint liability for contractors' wage violations, no piece-rate ban, and no federal registration regime. U.S. garment workers saw no change, and the domestic manufacturing grants were never funded.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Apparel brands and contractors, not garment workers

industries.note: As 'brand guarantors,' brands that contract for garment manufacturing would share legal liability for wage violations by any contractor or subcontractor doing their work, with workers able to recover lost wages plus equal liquidated damages. This would force brands to police wages deep into their supply chains or pay for violations themselves.

They would lose piece-rate pay systems and take on annual registration, fees starting at $200, detailed disclosure of owners and employees, and penalties up to $50 million. At the same time, compliant domestic shops become eligible for grants of up to $5 million, with priority for unionized, minority-, women-, and veteran-owned businesses.

The bill creates an Office of the Garment Industry at the Labor Department and authorizes $50 million in grants for training, equipment, and facility improvements at U.S. garment factories — a public investment aimed at keeping production, and the jobs that come with it, inside the country.
